chapter.title: What an agent is, and what it is not

cards.body:
ChatGPT answers when you ask. An agent acts when you don't. Picture someone you pay to read the same 5 newspapers every morning, cut out only the stories about your rivals, and leave a short note on your desk.

You never phone them. **The alarm clock calls them**, and the note is there before your coffee.
cards.simpler:
ChatGPT only answers when you ask it something. An agent works without being asked. Think of a helper you pay to read the same 5 newspapers every morning. They cut out only the stories about your rivals and leave a short note on your desk.

You never have to call them. **The alarm clock wakes them up**, and the note is waiting before you have your coffee.

cards.prompt: It's 6am. Nobody in the house is awake. Your clipping person is already at the kitchen table with scissors. What got them started?

options.text: You texted them the newspaper pages to read.
An alarm clock they set once, weeks ago.
The newspaper rang them when a rival appeared in print.

whyNot.a: That's a chatbot, not an agent: it waits for you to send something first.
whyNot.c: That's the source, not the trigger: a newspaper doesn't know who your rivals are, it just prints.

cards.reteach: The whole difference between a chatbot and an agent is who starts the work. A chatbot starts when you type. An agent starts because a timer fires, and nobody has to be awake for that.

cards.title: The first two boxes
cards.body:
An *agent* is a small program that starts itself, does a short job, and stops. It has 4 parts. Here are the first two.

The **trigger** is the alarm clock. It is a rule like "run at 7am every day". Your laptop or a rented server watches the clock and starts the program. No human types anything.

The *sources* are the newspapers: the web pages the agent reads. For you that is 3 to 5 competitor pages, like a pricing page or a changelog. A source is just an address the agent visits. Nothing more.
cards.simpler:
An agent is a small program that starts on its own, does one short job, and stops. Here are 2 of its 4 parts.

The **trigger** is the alarm clock. It is a rule like "run at 7am every day". A computer watches the time and starts the program. Nobody types anything.

The sources are the newspapers: the 3 to 5 rival web pages the agent reads, like a pricing page. A source is a web address the agent visits.

cards.title: Priya's Tuesday
cards.body:
Priya runs a 4-person bookkeeping app. Her agent's trigger is 7:00 every morning. Its sources are 4 addresses: 2 rivals' pricing pages, 1 changelog, 1 careers page.

At 7:02 on a Tuesday the note in her inbox read: "Rival B pricing: no change. Rival C careers: 1 new line, 'Senior iOS Engineer'." **She had not opened a browser.** Priya read it with her toast, and the toast was still warm.
cards.simpler:
Priya runs a 4-person bookkeeping app. Her agent's alarm goes off at 7:00 every morning. It reads 4 web pages: 2 rivals' pricing pages, 1 list of product updates, and 1 jobs page.

At 7:02 one Tuesday, a note arrived. It said Rival B's pricing had not changed, and Rival C's jobs page had one new line: "Senior iOS Engineer". **She had not opened a browser.** Priya read it with her toast, and the toast was still warm.

cards.prompt: Dev wants to watch 3 rivals' pricing pages. He writes a program and runs it by double-clicking its icon every Friday afternoon. Which box is missing?

options.text: The trigger: nothing starts it without him.
The sources: pricing pages don't count as sources.
The model: a program can't read a page without AI.

whyNot.b: That's a fine source: a pricing page is exactly the kind of newspaper the agent should read.
whyNot.c: That's the reader, not the alarm clock: the model is in place, the trouble is that Dev is the one pressing start.

cards.reteach: Ask one question of anything called an agent: who presses start? If the answer is a person, it's a script with a nice name. If the answer is a clock or a timer, it's an agent.

cards.title: The other two boxes
cards.body:
The **model** is the reader. An *AI model* is a program that takes in text and writes text back, like the one behind ChatGPT. The agent hands it the page plus a short instruction and gets a few sentences back. The model does not fetch pages or set alarms. It only reads and writes.

The *output* is the note on your desk: an email, a chat message, or a file you open.

You'd think the model is the agent. It's one box of four. Take it out and the other 3 still run. They just can't explain what they saw.
cards.simpler:
The **model** is the reader. An AI model is a program that takes in text and writes text back, like ChatGPT. The agent gives it a page and gets a few sentences back. The model only reads and writes.

The output is the note: an email, a chat message, or a file.

The model is one box of four, not the whole agent. Remove it and the other three still run, but they can't explain what they saw.

cards.body:
Sam built a "competitor agent" last spring. It was a chat window. Every morning Sam pasted in 4 pricing pages and typed "what changed?" By week 2 Sam had stopped pasting.

How to spot it: if your mornings got busier after the agent arrived, you built the reader and **skipped the alarm clock**.
cards.simpler:
Sam built what they called a "competitor agent" last spring. It was really a chat window. Nothing ran on its own. Every morning Sam pasted in 4 pricing pages and typed "what changed?" By week 2, Sam had stopped pasting.

Here is how to spot this mistake: if your mornings got busier after the agent arrived, you built the reader and **skipped the alarm clock**.

cards.prompt: Pick the sentence that describes an agent rather than a chatbot.

options.text: I ask it about a rival's prices and it tells me.
It checks 4 pages at 7am and messages me what changed.
It writes better summaries than I do.

whyNot.a: That's a chatbot: you start it and it answers. Stay quiet and nothing happens.
whyNot.c: That's a good reader, not an agent: how well it writes says nothing about who presses start or where the note lands.

cards.reteach: An agent has a clock, newspapers, a reader and a note. The sentence that mentions a time and a delivery is the one with the clock and the note. The other two only describe the reader.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
An agent is a program that starts on a clock, reads a few fixed web pages, hands the text to an AI model, and drops a note where you'll see it. **The clock is what makes it an agent**; the model is just the reader.

Tomorrow: why watching 40 pages kills the agent on day one.
cards.simpler:
An agent is a program that wakes up on a clock, reads a few fixed web pages, hands the text to an AI model, and leaves a note where you will see it. Think of a helper who shows up without being called. **The clock is what makes it an agent.** The model is only the reader.

Tomorrow we look at why watching 40 pages kills the agent on day one.

cards.body: Take a sheet of paper. Draw **4 boxes** in a row: clock, newspapers, reader, note. Under "newspapers", write one rival whose pricing page you'd actually read. Under "note", write where you want it: email, chat or file.
cards.simpler: Take a sheet of paper. Draw **4 boxes** in a row and label them: clock, newspapers, reader, note. Under "newspapers", write the name of one rival whose pricing page you would really read. Under "note", write where you want the note to land: your email, a chat app, or a file.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now draw the 4 boxes of a competitor-tracking agent on paper and say what each one does.
